cards.subject: math

objective.text: Sort and record data into a table using up to four categories. Use category counts to solve word problems.

explanations.title: Categories
explanations.text: A category is a group. We sort things into categories by their characteristics. A fish has scales and fins. A bird has feathers and wings.

explanations.title: A table organizes data
explanations.text: Data is information. A table puts data in rows. It is easier to count how many are in each category.

source_ref.section: Concept Development (organize our information, or data)

explanations.title: Tally marks
explanations.text: Make one tally mark for each thing. Count the marks to get the total. Then write the total as a number.

source_ref.section: Concept Development (record category counts using tally marks)

explanations.title: Tallies or numbers
explanations.text: Numbers give the total at once. Tally marks show the length of each group, so most and least are easy to see.

source_ref.section: Concept Development (which recording is easier to read)

explanations.title: Table direction
explanations.text: A table can go across or up and down. The data inside does not change.

source_ref.section: Concept Development (the orientation of the table)

explanations.title: How many more or fewer
explanations.text: To find how many more, compare two groups. Take away the same amount from both, or count the extra. A tape diagram can show it.

examples.title: Sort animals
examples.text: Sort animals as bird, mammal, reptile or fish. Make tally marks in each row. Then write each total as a number.

examples.title: Sort by habitat
examples.text: Sort the same animals by where they live: arctic, woodland or ocean. Record each count as a number.

examples.title: Penguins and whales
examples.text: 24 penguins and 18 whales. Compare the two. 24 minus 18 equals 6. There are 6 more penguins.

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Draw and label a picture graph to represent data with up to four categories.

explanations.title: Picture graph
explanations.text: A picture graph shows data with pictures. Each picture stands for one thing. The graph has a title, labels and a key.

explanations.title: Title and labels
explanations.text: The title tells what the graph is about. The labels name the categories. Write the labels in the same order as the table.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 1 (S: So we don't get confused)

explanations.title: A circle as a picture
explanations.text: A circle is a quick way to draw. Each circle stands for one thing. It is math, not art.

explanations.title: Legend or key
explanations.text: The legend, or key, tells what each picture stands for. For example, each circle stands for one animal.

explanations.title: More and fewer questions
explanations.text: Say the group with fewer first in 'how many fewer'. Say the group with more first in 'how many more'. The answer is the extra pictures.

explanations.title: Grid paper
explanations.text: Grid paper keeps the pictures in neat rows or columns. Fill only the squares above the labels.

examples.title: Animal Classification graph
examples.text: The title is Animal Classification. The categories are bird, mammal, reptile and fish. 4 circles are drawn for 4 birds. Each circle stands for one animal.

examples.title: Favorite Class of Animal
examples.text: Each child gets one vote. The votes are recorded in a table. Then a picture graph is made on grid paper.

examples.title: Robins, ducks and squirrels
examples.text: Gemma counts 16 robins, 19 ducks and 17 squirrels. 16 plus 19 equals 35. 35 minus 17 equals 18.

questions.text: I am holding up a coin worth 5 cents. What is the name of the coin?
How much is a nickel worth?
Gemma counts 16 robins, 19 ducks and 17 squirrels. How many robins and ducks are there in all?
How many more robins and ducks did Gemma count than squirrels?
What do we use to show data on a picture graph?
What is the title of a picture graph for the Animal Classification table?
Why do we write the labels in the same order as the table?
What quick shape do we draw in math drawings to stand for one thing?
The table says 4 birds. How many circles do you draw in the bird column?
What do we add to a graph to tell what each circle stands for?
In the animal graph, what does each circle stand for?
Why do we write the total for each category on the graph?
In 'how many fewer ___ are there than ___', which group do you say first?
In 'how many more ___ are there than ___', which group do you say first?
On a picture graph, how do you find 'how many more' mammals than fish?
Why is it called a picture graph? Are there pictures in the graph?
Why does grid paper make it easier to make a picture graph?
Does it matter if the circles go in rows or in columns? Does it change the information?
A picture graph has a title, labels and a legend. What else should be correct?
How does a picture graph help us organize information from a survey?
A zoo table shows birds 6, fish 5, mammals 11 and reptiles 3. How many more mammals than fish are there?
Use the same table. How many more mammals and fish are there than birds and reptiles?
How many fewer reptiles than mammals are there in that table?
A second zoo table shows birds 8, fish 4, mammals 12 and reptiles 5. How many more mammals than birds are there?
Use the same table. How many more mammals and reptiles are there than birds and fish?
How many fewer fish than birds are there in that table?
A vote for favorite mammal shows tiger 8, panda 11, snow leopard 7 and gorilla 12. How many more people chose gorilla than tiger?
Use the same vote. How many more people chose tiger and gorilla than panda and snow leopard?
How many fewer people chose tiger than panda?

objective.text: Draw a bar graph to represent a given data set.

explanations.title: Title, labels and scale first
explanations.text: Write the title first. Label the categories. Write the number scale. Then fill in the bars to match the table.

explanations.title: Horizontal and vertical bar graphs
explanations.text: A horizontal graph goes across and the scale is at the bottom. A vertical graph goes up and down and the scale is at the side. We compare how long or how tall the bars are.

explanations.title: The scale starts at 0
explanations.text: Like a ruler, the scale starts at 0. The space from 0 to the first line is a count of 1. We can turn the scale to go up like a ruler for height.

explanations.title: Comparison questions
explanations.text: To find how many more or fewer, compare the bars. You can subtract the two numbers.

source_ref.section: Student Debrief (what operation did you use?)

source_ref.section: Student Debrief (Do you think each box always has to be one unit?)

objective.text: Solve word problems using data presented in a bar graph.

explanations.title: Money in a graph
explanations.text: A bar graph can show money, like the number of dimes or nickels each child has. Read the bar to find each number.

explanations.title: Start the scale at 0
explanations.text: The scale starts at 0, not 1. A ruler helps you remember.

explanations.title: Find the total
explanations.text: To find the total, add all the numbers in the graph.

source_ref.section: Student Debrief (find the total amount of coins recorded)

explanations.title: Doubling
explanations.text: If a number doubles, add it to itself. To show a bigger number, add more boxes or let each box stand for 2.

explanations.title: Compare with a smaller unknown
explanations.text: 'More' can make you add, but sometimes you subtract. Draw a tape diagram to see which. Rita has 27 pennies, 19 more than Carlos. Carlos has fewer, so subtract.

examples.title: Rita and Carlos
examples.text: Rita has 27 pennies. That is 19 more than Carlos. 27 minus 19 equals 8. Carlos has 8 pennies.

examples.title: Callista's pennies
examples.text: Saturday 15, Sunday 10, Monday 4 and Tuesday 7. In all, 15 plus 10 plus 4 plus 7 equals 36 pennies.

objective.text: Recognize the value of coins and count up to find their total value.

explanations.title: Coin values
explanations.text: A penny is 1 cent. A nickel is 5 cents. A dime is 10 cents. A quarter is 25 cents.

explanations.title: Count the same coin
explanations.text: Skip-count to find the value of the same coins. Count nickels by fives and dimes by tens. 5 plus 5 plus 5 equals 15 for 3 nickels.

explanations.title: Start with the largest coin
explanations.text: To count mixed coins, start with the coin of largest value. Count the dimes by tens first. Then add the ones.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 2 (S: Counting the dimes first)

explanations.title: The cent sign
explanations.text: We write the value of coins with the cent sign. 23 cents is written 23¢. 100 cents can also be written $1.

explanations.title: Make a ten first
explanations.text: A quarter and a nickel make 30. Add the nickel to the quarter first. Then count on by tens and ones.

explanations.title: Decomposition tree
explanations.text: A decomposition tree breaks a whole into two parts. The two parts add up to the whole. 2 quarters make 50 cents, so each part is 25 cents.

examples.title: 2 dimes and 3 pennies
examples.text: Count the dimes first: 10, 20. Then the pennies: 21, 22, 23. The total is 23 cents.

examples.title: Quarter, nickel and penny
examples.text: 25 plus 5 equals 30. 30 plus 1 equals 31. The total is 31 cents.

examples.title: Make ten first
examples.text: 1 quarter, 3 dimes, 1 nickel, 2 pennies. 25 plus 5 is 30. Then 40, 50, 60. Then 61, 62. The total is 62 cents.

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Solve word problems involving different combinations of coins with the same total value.

explanations.title: Different coins, same value
explanations.text: Different coins can make the same value. A dime and 5 pennies is 15 cents. 3 nickels is also 15 cents.

explanations.title: Show an amount two ways
explanations.text: To show an amount two ways, use different coins. 28 cents is a quarter and 3 pennies. It is also 2 dimes and 8 pennies.

explanations.title: Trade coins
explanations.text: You can trade coins for other coins of the same value. Trade a quarter for 2 dimes and a nickel. The total stays the same.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 2 (S: I traded each of my quarters for 2 dimes and a nickel)

explanations.title: Tape diagram of coins
explanations.text: A tape diagram can show the value of each kind of coin as a part. The parts add up to the total value.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 2 (S: A tape diagram with one part 40 cents, one part 25 cents, and one part 10 cents)

explanations.title: Write the coins and the value
explanations.text: Write the coins you used and the total value. For example, 8 dimes and 3 pennies is 83 cents.

examples.title: 15 cents two ways
examples.text: A dime and 5 pennies is 15 cents. 3 nickels is 15 cents. The values are equal.

examples.title: Tony's 83 cents
examples.text: 8 dimes and 3 pennies is 83 cents. 3 quarters, 1 nickel and 3 pennies is also 83 cents.

examples.title: Carla and Peyton
examples.text: Carla has 4 dimes, 1 quarter and 2 nickels. That is 75 cents. Peyton has 3 coins with the same value. 25 plus 25 plus 25 is 75. Peyton has 3 quarters.

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Use the fewest number of coins to make a given value.

explanations.title: Fewest coins
explanations.text: It is easier to carry fewer coins. To use the fewest coins, use the coins with the greatest value.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 1 (S: use coins with the greatest possible value)

explanations.title: Trade for a bigger coin
explanations.text: Trade small coins for one coin of greater value. 2 dimes and 1 nickel trade for 1 quarter. 4 nickels trade for 2 dimes. You now have fewer coins.

explanations.title: Break the total into coin values
explanations.text: Break the total into as many twenty-fives as you can. Then tens. Then fives. Use pennies for what is left.

explanations.title: Tips for fewer coins
explanations.text: Do not use pennies if you can use a bigger coin. Use a dime instead of 2 nickels. Try a quarter because it is worth the most.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 1 (S: I didn't use pennies; a dime instead of 2 nickels; a quarter is worth the most)

examples.title: 40 cents
examples.text: 40 cents is 4 dimes. It is also 1 quarter and 3 nickels. Or 1 quarter, 1 dime and 1 nickel. The last way uses the fewest coins, 3.

examples.title: 35 cents: trade coins
examples.text: 3 dimes and 1 nickel is 4 coins. Trade 2 dimes and 1 nickel for 1 quarter. Now you have 1 quarter and 1 dime. That is 2 coins.

examples.title: 60 cents: trade coins
examples.text: 4 dimes and 4 nickels is 8 coins. Trade 4 dimes and 2 nickels for 2 quarters. Now you have 2 quarters and 1 dime. That is 3 coins.

examples.title: 27 cents
examples.text: 27 is 25 and 2 more. Use 1 quarter and 2 pennies. That is the fewest coins.

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Use different strategies to make 1 dollar or make change from 1 dollar.

explanations.title: 100 cents is 1 dollar
explanations.text: 100 cents is the same as 1 dollar. In a number sentence we can write 100 for the whole. We know the unit is cents.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 1 (S: 100 cents is just shown as the number 100)

explanations.title: Count up to a dollar
explanations.text: To find how much more you need to make 100 cents, count up from what you have. Use friendly numbers, like tens. The arrow way shows the jumps.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 1 (counting up with the arrow way)

explanations.title: Subtract from a dollar
explanations.text: You can also subtract from 100. 100 minus 30 is 70. Then take away the rest. Both ways find the missing part.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 1 (S: You can subtract 35 from 100. 100 minus 30 is 70, and 70 minus 5 is 65)

explanations.title: What is change?
explanations.text: Change is the money you get back at the store. You pay with more money than the cost. The cashier keeps the cost. The leftover money is your change.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 1 (what do you know about change)

explanations.title: Number bond for a dollar
explanations.text: A number bond for a dollar has 1 dollar, or 100 cents, as the whole. One part is the money you know. The other part is the missing money.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 2 (number bond; the whole is $1, one part is 17 cents)

examples.title: 35 cents to a dollar
examples.text: You have a quarter and a dime. That is 35 cents. Add a nickel to make 40. Add a dime to make 50. Add 2 quarters to make 100. You need 65 cents more.

examples.title: 28 cents from a dollar
examples.text: You have 28 cents. Count up by dimes and then pennies: 38, 48, 58, 68, 78, 88, 98, 99, 100. 28 plus 72 makes 100. You have 72 cents left.

examples.title: 17 cents and the hidden coins
examples.text: One part is 17 cents. The whole is 1 dollar. 17 plus 83 makes 100. The hidden money is 83 cents.

examples.title: Candy and change
examples.text: You start with 1 dollar. You get 66 cents back as change. Count up from 66: 70, 75, 100. The candy costs 34 cents.

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Solve word problems about different ways to make change from 1 dollar.

explanations.title: 1 dollar is 100 cents
explanations.text: A dollar is the same as 100 cents. You can write 100 cents as $1 in a number sentence. So 24 cents and a missing amount can make $1.

explanations.title: Find the change
explanations.text: Change is the money you get back. Take the cost away from 1 dollar. Or count on from the cost up to 1 dollar. Both ways find the change.

explanations.title: Find the cost from the change
explanations.text: Sometimes you know the change. Find the value of the change coins. The cost and the change are the two parts of 1 dollar. Take the change from 1 dollar to find the cost.

explanations.title: Take one from both numbers
explanations.text: Take 1 away from both numbers to make a problem that is easier. 100 minus 57 has the same answer as 99 minus 56. You do not need to rename.

explanations.title: Check your answer
explanations.text: Reread the problem. Add the cost and the change. They should make 100 cents, or 1 dollar. If they do not, check again.

explanations.title: Dollars and cents
explanations.text: A dollar is made of 100 cents. This is like a hundred made of ten tens. We can trade 1 dollar for 100 cents.

examples.title: Shay buys a balloon
examples.text: The balloon costs 57 cents. Shay hands over 1 dollar. 57 cents plus 43 cents equals 100 cents. Shay gets 43 cents in change.

examples.title: Jamie's baseball card
examples.text: Jamie gets 2 dimes, 1 quarter and 1 penny in change. That is 46 cents. 100 minus 46 equals 54. The card cost 54 cents.

examples.title: Penelope's toy whistle
examples.text: Penelope has 15 pennies, 2 nickels, 2 dimes and 1 quarter. That is 70 cents. The whistle costs 1 dollar. She needs 30 more cents.

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Solve two-step word problems about dollars or cents, with totals within 100 dollars or 1 dollar.

explanations.title: Draw a model first
explanations.text: Before you solve, think about the model. A tape diagram or a number bond shows the parts and the whole. Think about the operation and a strategy too.

explanations.title: Find the missing coin
explanations.text: Find the value of the coins you know. Count up or subtract to reach the new total. The difference is the value of the missing coin.

explanations.title: Two steps
explanations.text: Some problems have two parts. Find one amount first. Then use it to find the answer. Use two tape diagrams of the same size, and make one longer for the extra.

explanations.title: Find the start
explanations.text: When money was spent and some is left, the cost and the money left are two parts. Add them to find what you had at the start.

explanations.title: Skip-count the money
explanations.text: Skip-count by tens, then fives, then ones. For bills, skip-count by fives and ones. This helps you find one part quickly.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Parts 1 and 3; Student Debrief

explanations.title: 100 cents in nickels
explanations.text: 100 cents is the same as 20 nickels. You can also find the value of the coins and take it from 100.

examples.title: Gary's missing coin
examples.text: Gary has 2 dimes, 5 nickels and 13 pennies. That is 58 cents. A coin from his brother makes 68 cents. 68 minus 58 equals 10. The coin is a dime.

examples.title: Hailey's snack
examples.text: The pretzel stick costs a dime and a nickel, or 15 cents. The juice box costs 18 cents more, so it costs 33 cents. 15 plus 33 equals 48. Hailey spent 48 cents.

examples.title: Wendell's game
examples.text: Wendell has 2 five-dollar bills and 4 one-dollar bills left. That is 14 dollars. The game cost 16 dollars. 16 plus 14 equals 30. He had 30 dollars at the start.

questions.text: In a decomposition tree, 100 is the whole. One part is 60. What is the other part?
In a decomposition tree, 100 is the whole. One part is 35. What is the other part?
In a decomposition tree, 100 is the whole. One part is 82. What is the other part?
Dante had some money in a jar. He puts 8 nickels into the jar. Now he has 100 cents. How much money was in the jar at first, in cents?
Gary has 2 dimes, 5 nickels and 13 pennies. How many cents is that?
Gary's brother gives him one more coin. Now Gary has 68 cents. What coin did his brother give him?
Hailey bought a pretzel stick for a dime and a nickel. How many cents did it cost?
Hailey's juice box cost 18 cents more than the pretzel stick. How much did the juice box cost, in cents?
How much did Hailey spend on the pretzel stick and the juice box, in cents?
Wendell has 2 five-dollar bills and 4 one-dollar bills left after buying a game. How many dollars is that?
Wendell bought a game for 16 dollars. He has 14 dollars left. How many dollars did he have before he bought the game?
Josephine has 3 nickels, 4 dimes and 12 pennies. Her mother gives her 1 coin. Now Josephine has 92 cents. What coin did her mother give her?
Christopher has 3 ten-dollar bills, 3 five-dollar bills and 12 one-dollar bills. Jenny has 19 dollars more than Christopher. How many dollars does Jenny have?
Isaiah started with 2 twenty-dollar bills, 4 ten-dollar bills, 1 five-dollar bill and 7 one-dollar bills. He spent 73 dollars on clothes. How many dollars does he have left?
Jackie bought a sweater for 42 dollars. She had 3 five-dollar bills and 6 one-dollar bills left over. How many dollars did she have before she bought the sweater?
Mary found 98 cents in her piggy bank. She counted 1 quarter, 8 pennies, 3 dimes and some nickels. How many nickels did she count?
Akio found 18 cents in one pocket. He found 6 more coins in his other pocket. Altogether he has 73 cents. How many cents are the 6 coins worth?
Akio's 6 coins in his other pocket are worth 55 cents. What could the 6 coins be?
Gary went to the store with 4 ten-dollar bills, 3 five-dollar bills and 7 one-dollar bills. He bought a sweater for 26 dollars. How many dollars does he have left?
Gary has 36 dollars left after he bought a sweater. What bills could he have left the store with?
Kelly bought a pencil sharpener for 47 cents and a pencil for 35 cents. What was her change from 1 dollar, in cents?
Hae Jung bought a pretzel for 3 dimes and a nickel. She also bought a juice box. She spent 92 cents. How much was the juice box, in cents?
Monique saved 2 ten-dollar bills, 4 five-dollar bills and 15 one-dollar bills. Harry saved 16 dollars more than Monique. How many dollars did Harry save?
Ryan went shopping with 3 twenty-dollar bills, 3 ten-dollar bills, 1 five-dollar bill and 9 one-dollar bills. He spent 59 dollars on a video game. How many dollars does he have left?
Heather had 3 ten-dollar bills and 4 five-dollar bills left after buying sneakers for 29 dollars. How many dollars did she have before she bought the sneakers?
Nolan has 1 quarter, 1 nickel and 21 pennies. His brother gave him 2 coins. Now he has 86 cents. What 2 coins did his brother give him?
Before you solve a word problem, what should you think about?
How can skip-counting help you solve one part of a money problem quickly?
How did a tape diagram or number bond help you solve a problem today?

objective.text: Measure with an inch tile by laying one unit end to end with no gaps.

explanations.title: Mark and move forward
explanations.text: Put the unit at the start of the line. Mark where it ends. Move the unit forward so its edge sits on the mark. Keep going until the whole line is measured.

explanations.title: No gaps
explanations.text: Do not leave any space between the units. Use the same size unit every time. The spaces between the hash marks are all the same length.

explanations.title: The inch tile
explanations.text: An inch tile is a length unit called an inch. It is bigger than a centimeter cube. You can use it the same way as a centimeter cube.

explanations.title: About how long
explanations.text: A line may not be an exact number of tiles. If it is half a tile longer or more, say about the next number. If it is less than half a tile longer, say about the number you counted.

explanations.title: Big units and small units
explanations.text: A larger unit covers a length faster. You use fewer of them. A smaller unit takes more moves. Always use the same size unit to compare two lengths.

explanations.title: Count units, not marks
explanations.text: Count the length units between the marks. Do not count the hash marks. A line with 5 marks has 4 units between them.

source_ref.section: Student Debrief (counted hash marks instead of length units)

examples.text: Frances uses a book to measure. The bookcase is 5 books long. The space is 4 books long. The bookcase will not fit.

examples.title: A 4 inch tile line
examples.text: A line has a hash mark at each end. The tile is moved forward 4 times. The spaces between the marks are all the same length. The line is 4 inch tiles long.

objective.text: Make an inch ruler and use it to measure lengths.

explanations.title: Make an inch ruler
explanations.text: Lay an inch tile at the left end of the strip. Draw a line where it ends. Write 1 above the line. Keep moving the tile with no gaps. Write each number above its mark.

explanations.title: What 0 means
explanations.text: Write 0 at the left edge. It means you have not measured anything yet. It is where you start to measure.

explanations.title: What each number means
explanations.text: Each number tells how many inches you have measured so far. The number 1 is one length unit. The end of a 2 inch paper clip is at the number 2.

explanations.title: A foot
explanations.text: The last number on the ruler is 12. 12 inches make a larger unit called a foot. 12 inches equals 1 foot.

explanations.title: Units inside units
explanations.text: A foot is made of 12 inches. A ten is made of 10 ones. A hundred is made of 10 tens. A dollar is made of 100 cents.

explanations.title: Why use a ruler
explanations.text: A ruler keeps all the inches together. You can measure all at once. This is faster than moving one tile again and again.

explanations.title: Unit size and number
explanations.text: The smaller the length unit, the more of them you need. The larger the length unit, the fewer you need.

explanations.title: Add inches to make a foot
explanations.text: To add 9 inches and 6 inches, make a foot first. 9 needs 3 more to make 12. Then 3 are left over. So you get 1 foot 3 inches.

examples.title: A 2 inch paper clip
examples.text: Lay the paper clip along the ruler from 0. It ends at 2. The paper clip is 2 inches long. A line drawn from 0 to 2 is the same length.

examples.title: A 5 inch index card
examples.text: The index card ends at 5 on the ruler. It is 5 inches long. 5 inches plus 7 inches equals 12 inches, or 1 foot.

examples.title: Edwin and Tina's truck
examples.text: Edwin measures with toothpicks and gets 4. Tina measures with lima beans and gets 12. A bean is a smaller unit, so she needs more of them. Both are right.

objective.text: Measure objects with a 12-inch ruler and a yardstick. Pick the unit and the tool that fit the object.

explanations.title: Inch, foot and yard
explanations.text: An inch is a small unit. A foot is 12 inches. A yard is 3 feet. A 12-inch ruler measures 1 foot.

explanations.title: Pick a unit that fits
explanations.text: Small things, like a pencil, fit inches. Longer things, like a rug, fit feet. Very long things, like a street, fit yards.

explanations.title: Pick a tool that fits
explanations.text: A 12-inch ruler is good for short objects. A yardstick is good for long objects. A long object needs fewer moves with a yardstick.

explanations.title: A yardstick is 3 feet
explanations.text: Every yardstick length is 3 feet. Lay a yardstick 2 times to measure 2 yardsticks. That is 3 feet plus 3 feet.

explanations.title: One yardstick, three units
explanations.text: You can measure in inches, feet or yards with a yardstick. Pick the unit that fits the object.

explanations.title: Compare to a yardstick
explanations.text: Before you measure, guess. Is the object more than, less than, or about the same length as the yardstick?

examples.title: Billy's pencil
examples.text: Billy says his pencil is 7 feet long. A foot is long, so this is too long. A pencil fits inches. He can say 7 inches.

examples.title: Yardstick laid 2 times
examples.text: A rug is 2 yardsticks long. Each yardstick is 3 feet. 3 plus 3 is 6. The rug is 6 feet long.

objective.text: Estimate lengths with mental benchmarks. Then measure to check your estimate.

explanations.title: Mental benchmarks
explanations.text: A mental benchmark is an object you know the length of. Use it to think about other lengths. A quarter is about an inch. A sheet of paper is about a foot. A door width is about a yard.

explanations.title: Estimate, then measure
explanations.text: Step 1: Pick a mental benchmark and estimate. Step 2: Measure to see how close you are.

explanations.title: Compare to the benchmark
explanations.text: Find the benchmark closest in length to the object. Is the object a little more or a little less? A lot more or a lot less?

explanations.title: Picture the benchmark again and again
explanations.text: See how many times the benchmark fits along the object. That helps you estimate the length.

explanations.title: Why benchmarks help
explanations.text: If someone says a room is about 10 yards long, a benchmark helps you picture it. Benchmarks help you understand sizes.

examples.title: Estimate a marker
examples.text: Estimates for the marker: 7 inches and 5 inches. The marker is shorter than the paper but longer than a quarter. You measure it. It is 8 inches.

examples.title: Benjamin's arms
examples.text: Forearm is 15 inches. Upper arm is 15 inches. One arm is 15 plus 15, which is 30 inches. Both arms are 30 plus 30, which is 60 inches.

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Measure one object with two different length units and compare. See how the size of the unit changes the number.

explanations.title: Same object, two units
explanations.text: Measure one pencil with an inch ruler and a centimeter ruler. You get two different numbers. Both are correct. The units are different.

explanations.title: Smaller unit, more units
explanations.text: A centimeter is smaller than an inch. It takes more centimeters to cover the same length. The smaller the unit, the more units you need.

explanations.title: Bigger unit, fewer units
explanations.text: An inch is bigger than a centimeter. The bigger the unit, the fewer units you use.

explanations.title: 5 inches and 5 centimeters
explanations.text: Draw a line 5 inches long and a line 5 centimeters long. The 5-inch line is longer. One inch is longer than one centimeter.

explanations.title: Use what you know
explanations.text: 13 centimeters is about 5 inches. A line with more than 13 centimeters is longer than 5 inches. You do not have to measure again.

explanations.title: Break apart 20 inches
explanations.text: A decomposition tree breaks a whole into two parts. The two parts add up to the whole. You can break 20 inches in many ways.

examples.title: The pencil
examples.text: The pencil is about 7 inches long. It is about 18 centimeters long. Both are correct. We need more centimeters because they are smaller.

examples.title: Thomas and Chris
examples.text: Thomas says the crayon is 8 centimeters. Chris says it is 3 inches. Both are right. They used different units.

objective.text: Measure two lengths and find how much longer or shorter one is. Use inches, feet and yards.

explanations.title: Find the difference
explanations.text: To compare two lengths, measure both. Then subtract the smaller length from the bigger length. The answer is how much longer one is.

explanations.title: Add on to find the difference
explanations.text: You can add on from the shorter length to the longer length. 17 plus 3 is 20. 20 plus 12 is 32. 3 plus 12 is 15.

explanations.title: Pick a tool and a unit
explanations.text: A yardstick can measure in inches, feet or yards. Use inches for short things. Use feet for longer things. Use yards for very long things.

explanations.title: Between two marks
explanations.text: If a length is between two marks, look at which mark is closer. More than halfway, say the next number. Less than halfway, say the smaller number.

explanations.title: Unit size changes the difference
explanations.text: The string and wall do not change. Feet are smaller than yards. We need more feet than yards to cover the same length.

examples.title: Paper and desk
examples.text: The desktop is 24 inches. The paper is 30 inches. The paper is longer. 30 minus 24 is 6. The paper is 6 inches longer.

examples.title: String and wall
examples.text: The string is 17 feet. The wall is 32 feet. 32 minus 17 is 15. You need 15 more feet of string. In yards, the difference is 5 yards.

objective.text: Solve word problems about length. Use tape diagrams and number sentences.

explanations.title: Tape diagram for how many more
explanations.text: Draw one tape for the length now and one for the length you want. Put a question mark on the part you do not know. Then write a number sentence.

explanations.title: Change yards to inches
explanations.text: Sometimes the problem uses two units. One yard is 36 inches. Change the yard to inches before you find the answer.

explanations.title: Two-step problems
explanations.text: Some problems need two steps. First find a length that is missing. Then answer the question that was asked. Reread the problem to check the question.

explanations.title: Difference in a tape diagram
explanations.text: When a rope is 18 inches shorter, 18 is the difference. It is not the length of the short rope. Put the question mark where the total length is.

explanations.title: Draw the triangle
explanations.text: Draw the shape in the story. Two sides are the same length, so write the same number on both. Label the total and the question mark.

explanations.title: Make a ten to add
explanations.text: To add 42 and 19, take 1 from 42. Give it to 19 to make 20. Then add 41 and 20.

examples.title: The scarf
examples.text: The scarf is 19 inches long now. He wants 36 inches. 19 plus what number equals 36? Count up 1 to 20, then 16 more. He needs 17 more inches.

examples.title: The two ropes
examples.text: One rope is 64 inches. The shorter rope is 18 inches less. 64 minus 18 equals 46. Then 64 plus 46 equals 110. Both ropes are 110 inches.

examples.title: The triangle
examples.text: The sides add up to 96 feet. Two sides are 40 feet each. 40 plus 40 equals 80. 96 minus 80 equals 16. The last side is 16 feet.

objective.text: Find unknown numbers on a number line. Use the distance between numbers and points you know.

explanations.title: Endpoints and zooming in
explanations.text: A number line has a left endpoint and a right endpoint. The left endpoint is often 0. You can zoom in on one piece, like 30 to 50. The other numbers are still there, just not written.

explanations.title: Hash marks and units
explanations.text: Hash marks are the small lines. A unit is the space between two hash marks. Count the spaces to count units. 5 hash marks make 4 units.

explanations.title: Find points with the unit value
explanations.text: Every unit on a number line has the same length. If you know one unit, you know them all. Count by that unit from a point you know to find the missing point.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Problem 1 and 2; Student Debrief

explanations.title: Cut a length in half
explanations.text: A hash mark in the middle is the same distance from both ends. Between 30 and 50 the middle is 40. Cut each half again to make 4 equal units of 5.

explanations.title: Difference between endpoints
explanations.text: Add the unit lengths to find the total distance. You can also subtract the small endpoint from the big endpoint. Both ways give the same difference.

examples.title: Number line from 30 to 50
examples.text: The endpoints are 30 and 50. There are 4 units. Each unit is 5. Count by fives: 30, 35, 40, 45, 50. Point A is 35 and Point B is 45. The difference is 20.

examples.title: Count up from 100
examples.text: A number line starts at 100. It has 4 units of 10. Count by tens: 100, 110, 120, 130, 140. Point E is 140. The difference is 40.

examples.title: Count back from 95
examples.text: A number line ends at 95. It has 4 units of 10. Count back by tens from 95. Point A is 55. The difference is 40.

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Use a ruler as a number line to show sums and differences about length.

explanations.title: More length means add
explanations.text: To show 20 more than 35, start at 35. Slide right 20. Count by fives or tens. Where you stop is the answer. 35 plus 20 equals 55.

explanations.title: Less length means subtract
explanations.text: To show 15 less than 55, start at 55. Slide left 15. Where you stop is the answer. 55 minus 15 equals 40.

explanations.title: Length of an object
explanations.text: Put one end of the object at one endpoint. The length is the distance from the left end to the right end. Count the units, or subtract the two endpoints.

explanations.title: Slide the object to make it easier
explanations.text: Sliding an object does not change its length. Slide it so one end is on a ten. 62 minus 49 is the same as 63 minus 50. Both equal 13.

explanations.title: Count jumps, not marks
explanations.text: Know how long each unit is. Skip-count by that length. Count the jumps, not the hash marks.

explanations.title: Make a hundred to add
explanations.text: To add 420 and 190, take 10 from 420. Give it to 190 to make 200. Then add 410 and 200.

examples.title: 20 more than 35

examples.title: Length of the pencil
examples.text: A pencil goes from 49 to 62. 62 minus 49 equals 13. Slide it 1 unit right. Now it goes from 50 to 63. 63 minus 50 equals 13. The pencil is 13 units long.

objective.text: Measure and record data in a table. Answer questions about the data and tell what it shows.

explanations.title: Measure your handspan
explanations.text: Your handspan is the length from your pinky tip to your thumb tip. Stretch your fingers out. Start measuring at zero on the ruler. Say about how many inches it is.

explanations.title: Record data with tally marks
explanations.text: Each person gets one tally mark in the row for their handspan. Count the tally marks in a row to know how many people have that handspan.

explanations.title: Most common and least common
explanations.text: The most common handspan has the most tally marks. The least common handspan has the fewest tally marks.

explanations.title: Ask a comparison question
explanations.text: A comparison question asks how many more. To answer it, subtract the smaller count from the bigger count. Use the numbers in the table.

explanations.title: 100 more than
explanations.text: 300 minus 200 is 100. So 100 more than 200 is 300. Say the subtraction as a how many more sentence.

examples.title: Comparing handspans
examples.text: Suppose 7 people have a handspan of 5 inches and 2 people have 8 inches. 7 minus 2 equals 5. 5 more people have a handspan of 5 inches than 8 inches.

objective.text: Draw a line plot to show measurement data. Relate the measurement scale to the number line.

explanations.title: What a line plot is
explanations.text: A line plot shows data on a number line. Put an X above the number for each measurement. Write the unit. Give the plot a title, like a bar graph.

explanations.title: From tally marks to X's
explanations.text: Each tally mark in the table becomes one X. Every X is the same size. Stack the X's above the number.

explanations.title: Data may not start at zero
explanations.text: Sometimes the data start at a number like 3. Two slashes show that some numbers are skipped. The first label is the shortest measurement. The last label is the longest.

explanations.title: Label every number
explanations.text: Label every number from the shortest to the longest. Do this even when no item has that measure. The steps on a number line must be equal. An empty spot shows a gap in the data.

explanations.title: A ruler is a number line
explanations.text: One box on centimeter grid paper is 1 centimeter. The centimeters on a ruler are like the numbers on a number line. Your line plot can match the ruler.

examples.title: Shoe lengths
examples.text: The shortest shoe is 19 centimeters. The longest is 26 centimeters. No shoe is 23 or 24 centimeters. Still label 19 to 26 on the number line.

examples.title: Handspans
examples.text: The handspan number line goes from 3 to 8 inches. It has two slashes after zero. Each tally mark becomes an X above its number of inches.

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Draw a line plot for a data set. Answer questions and draw conclusions from measurement data.

explanations.title: Start with the table
explanations.text: Find the smallest and the greatest measurement in the table. The number line goes from the smallest to the greatest. Label every number between, even with no data.

explanations.title: Draw the line plot
explanations.text: Draw a number line. Label it with the unit. Put one X above the number for each measurement. Make every X the same size. Add a title.

explanations.title: Ask questions of a line plot
explanations.text: The most common measurement has the tallest stack of X's. The difference is the greatest minus the smallest. The total is the number of X's. An X far from the rest is outside the main group.

explanations.title: Table or line plot
explanations.text: A table organizes data. A line plot lets you compare the amounts at a glance.

explanations.title: Fewer than
explanations.text: To find a number that is fewer than a total, add the parts first. Then take away the amount fewer. A tape diagram helps.

examples.title: Bean plants
examples.text: Bean plant heights go from 9 to 15 cm. No plant is 10 cm, so 10 has no X. The most common height is 13 cm. The difference between tallest and shortest is 6 cm. There are 26 plants.

examples.title: Sit and reach
examples.text: Reach distances go from 22 to 34 cm. No student is 24, 32 or 33 cm, so those have no X. The most common reach is 28 cm. The difference is 12 cm.

objective.text: Draw a line plot for a data set. Answer questions and draw conclusions from measurement data.

explanations.title: Start at zero with slashes
explanations.text: Write 0 at the start of the scale. Add two slashes after it. The slashes show that the numbers before the first label are not shown. Then label up to the greatest measurement.

explanations.title: Label the unit
explanations.text: Label the scale with the unit of the measuring tool. Look at the table to find the unit. Then put an X above the number for each measurement.

explanations.title: Thermometer
explanations.text: A thermometer is a tool that measures temperature. We measure temperature in degrees. The numbers on a thermometer go up and down.

explanations.title: Vertical line plot
explanations.text: A line plot can have a vertical scale. Then the number line goes up and down. The X's go next to the numbers, in a row. The data stay the same.

explanations.title: When a table is easier
explanations.text: A line plot is easy to read when the numbers are close together. When the numbers are far apart, a table can be easier.

explanations.title: Make the next hundred
explanations.text: To add, make the next hundred first. Move some from the second number to the first. Then add what is left.
